clue.text: Pub's bill for wine

parts.note: a pub is a bar, and the possessive keeps its S
AC is the abbreviation for account, a bill

explanation.surface: A drinker settles the tab for some wine at the local.
explanation.definitionFit: Barsac is a sweet white Bordeaux from the Sauternes district.

clue.text: Place the poor actor bleats about

indicators.note: the bleating noise sits around the actor, so 'about' asks for one piece wrapped round the other

parts.note: sheep bleat, giving their cry in the plural
a ham is a poor, overacting performer

explanation.surface: A bad actor's whining sounds like a flock of sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts HAM inside BAAS, splitting it BA...AS.
explanation.definitionFit: The islands of the Bahamas are a country, so a place on the map.

clue.text: Obviously guilty, with a fistful of diamonds?

explanation.surface: A card cheat is caught holding a suspiciously good hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Diamonds are a red suit in cards, so a hand full of them is literally a red hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Caught in the act of wrongdoing; and, taken literally, holding a hand of the red suit.

clue.text: Drive to a meeting place?

parts.note: a venue is where people gather for an event

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a lift to wherever the gathering is held.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' looks like a verb; it is a road name, as in 'Park Drive'.
explanation.definitionFit: A drive and an avenue are both kinds of road, often tree-lined.

clue.text: Supporter leaped exultantly about the street

indicators.note: the jumbled word goes round the road abbreviation, so 'about' means surrounding
leaping exultantly suggests wild, disordered motion, so the letters of leaped are tossed about

explanation.surface: A fan jumped for joy all around the road after a win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exultantly' turns LEAPED into PEDEAL, and 'about' puts ST inside it: PEDE-ST-AL.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestal is the base that holds up a statue or column, a physical support.

clue.text: A mis-shapen nose ages

indicators.note: a misshapen nose is bent out of its proper form, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A crooked nose becomes more noticeable as a person grows old.
explanation.definitionFit: Eons are immensely long periods, as are ages.

clue.text: Times are changing for Arab states

indicators.note: times that are changing are being altered, so these letters change their order

explanation.surface: Echoes the song: political times are shifting across the Arab world.
explanation.definitionFit: The United Arab Emirates is a federation of seven Gulf sheikhdoms, Arab states each ruled by an emir.

clue.text: The main idea of work, perhaps

explanation.surface: Someone asks what a piece of writing is really about.
explanation.walkthrough: A theme is the subject of a piece, and also a school essay or composition, a piece of work.
explanation.definitionFit: The central subject of a discussion; and a short written composition set as homework.

clue.text: Goes flat out arranging tenancies to rent

parts.note: a landlord arranging tenancies makes lets of property
rent as a verb means to tear, which is to rip

explanation.surface: A landlord is frantically busy fixing up rental agreements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like paying for a flat; here it is the past of 'rend', to tear.
explanation.definitionFit: To let rip is to go at full speed or with no restraint.

clue.text: Acted evasively, being naturally guarded

explanation.surface: A shifty character dodges questions while keeping well protected.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a field or garden enclosed by a hedge, a natural barrier.
explanation.definitionFit: Avoided committing oneself; and fenced in by living shrubs.

clue.text: The sort of speech that gets reported

definitions.text: The sort of speech that gets reported

parts.words: The sort of speech that gets reported
parts.note: grammar term for a speaker's words retold with 'he said that...' rather than quoted

explanation.definitionFit: Indirect speech is the grammatical name for reported speech.

clue.text: Bowl with hand over'

explanation.surface: A cricket captain gives the ball to a bowler for the next over.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket to bowl a ball is to deliver it; an 'over' is a set of six balls, which makes the surface a cricket scene.
explanation.definitionFit: To send the ball at the batter; and to pass something to someone.

clue.text: Hands and feet, for example

parts.note: body parts are really units: a hand gauges a horse's height, a foot is twelve inches

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands and feet' look like body parts; both are units of length.
explanation.definitionFit: Hands and feet are units used to state length or height.

clue.text: Rush into a job for life

explanation.surface: Someone dashes headlong into permanent employment.
explanation.definitionFit: To move swiftly and uncontrolled; and a lifelong profession.

clue.text: Retribution seems in order

indicators.note: putting things in order rearranges them, so these letters are sorted afresh

explanation.surface: Someone thinks punishment is fully deserved.
explanation.definitionFit: Nemesis is deserved downfall or vengeance, after the Greek goddess of vengeance.

clue.text: Bias shown by the team

explanation.surface: A referee shows favouritism toward the home players.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker and billiards side is spin, a bias put on the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Spin given to a ball, a bias; and a team in a match.

clue.text: Generally helpful, he has the odd idea to abscond

indicators.note: an odd idea is strange or out of shape, so its letters are put in a new arrangement

parts.note: to decamp is to run away secretly

explanation.surface: A useful fellow has a strange notion of running off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' turns IDEA into AIDE. 'Generally helpful' means helpful to a general, the officer such an assistant serves.
explanation.definitionFit: An aide-de-camp is an officer who assists a senior commander.

clue.text: Possibly meant to go round some accommodation

indicators.note: the reworked letters surround the next piece, so 'to go round' means enclosing it
'possibly' says the word meant may be in another form, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: part means some of something

explanation.surface: Someone intended to view a few places to live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' turns MEANT into AMENT, and 'to go round' puts PART inside it: A-PART-MENT.
explanation.definitionFit: An apartment is a flat, a set of rooms to live in.

clue.text: Biased team and what may be done about it

indicators.note: the reshuffled letters are placed around the team, so 'about' means surrounding
the word done may be in another form, so its letters are reshuffled

parts.note: a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: A partial referee prompts the question of what can be done about the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' turns DONE into ONED, and 'about' puts SIDE inside it: ONE-SIDE-D.
explanation.definitionFit: Partial, favouring only one party in a dispute.

clue.text: Finished full of wrath and in jeopardy

indicators.note: the first word contains the second, so 'full of' signals one piece holding the other

parts.note: finished means ended
wrath is anger

explanation.surface: Someone ends a quarrel furious and at risk.
explanation.definitionFit: An endangered thing is at risk of harm or extinction.

clue.text: Letter that is spelt badly

indicators.note: something spelt badly has its letters in the wrong order, so these are rearranged

parts.note: IE is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A complaint that a letter is full of spelling mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges IE and SPELT together.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a formal letter, as in the New Testament epistles.

clue.text: Beheaded, it would be even more venomous

definitions.text: Beheaded, it would be even more venomous

parts.words: Beheaded, it would be even more venomous
parts.note: a stinging insect whose name, with its first letter cut off, leaves a deadly snake

explanation.walkthrough: Take off the first letter and the insect becomes the ASP, a venomous snake.
explanation.definitionFit: A stinging insect whose name minus its head letter is a venomous snake.

clue.text: Knock up a note before ten? It can be true

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means the word is read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: a knock is a rap
do is the first note of the sol-fa scale
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: Someone knocks a note together before ten, a puzzling claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns RAP into PAR in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: A paradox is a statement that seems absurd yet may prove well founded.

clue.text: Snooker on the green?

parts.note: to snooker is to block; on a golf green a ball lying between another and the hole blocks it

explanation.walkthrough: In old golf rules a ball blocking an opponent's line to the hole was this; 'snooker' means to obstruct.
explanation.definitionFit: To stymie is to obstruct, originally a golf term for a blocking ball on the green.

clue.text: I'm taking a certain attitude for tax

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
a pose is a deliberate posture or attitude

explanation.surface: Someone strikes a stance about taxation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tax' is a verb here: to impose a burden.
explanation.definitionFit: To impose is to levy a duty or burden, as a tax is.

clue.text: Manufactured pearl is not so lustrous

indicators.note: a manufactured pearl is made artificially, so its letters are made into a new word

explanation.surface: An artificial pearl lacks the shine of a real one.
explanation.definitionFit: Paler means less bright, with less sheen.

clue.text: This ruler won't give an inch

definitions.text: This ruler won't give an inch

parts.words: This ruler won't give an inch
parts.note: a ruler here is an autocrat who never concedes, not a measuring stick marked in inches

explanation.walkthrough: 'ruler' and 'inch' suggest a measuring rule; the ruler is a tyrant who never compromises.
explanation.definitionFit: An absolute ruler who will not concede the smallest point.

clue.text: In tennis Wimbledon is one way to make sporting progress

definitions.text: one way to make sporting progress

indicators.note: 'In' says the letters sit within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Winning at Wimbledon is one route to advancing in sport.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across tenniS WIMbledon.
explanation.definitionFit: Swimming is a way of moving through water, a sport.

clue.text: Be patronising in speech and overbearing in argument

explanation.surface: Someone condescends when chatting and bullies when debating.
explanation.walkthrough: To talk down to someone is to patronise; to talk someone down is to silence them by force of argument.
explanation.definitionFit: To address someone condescendingly; and to defeat someone by louder, insistent argument.

clue.text: Threaten one politician with death

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
MP is a Member of Parliament
end is a word for death

explanation.surface: A single politician is threatened with being killed.
explanation.definitionFit: To impend is to hang over as a menace, to loom.

clue.text: They may give me a lord's estates

indicators.note: the words may give a different result when rearranged, so their letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: Someone hopes to inherit a nobleman's lands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may give' rearranges ME A LORDS, keeping the S of the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Earldoms are the territories or titles held by earls, so lands of nobility.

clue.text: Divert expedition around summit

indicators.note: 'around' says the answer lies inside the words, which surround it

explanation.surface: Redirect the climbing party round the peak.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across diVERT EXpedition.
explanation.definitionFit: A vertex is the highest point, the apex.
